name: Nafsan
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Research on the prosodic characteristics of Nafsan is ongoing, but indications are that there is a strong preference for words to be more prominent at the right edge. Analyses of disyllabic and trisyllabic words produced in an utterance-medial frame show a clear pattern of higher fundamental frequency values in final compared to preceding syllables (Billington et al. 2018, 2020). [...] This suggests that syllable weight does not influence the location of prominence within the word. [...] While previous descriptions of Nafsan have discussed various possible prominence patterns as lexical stress, there is emerging evidence that accentual prominence in Nafsan may be phrasal.
new_statements.citation: Billington, Rosey, Nick Thieberger & Janet Fletcher. 2023 [online 2021]. Nafsan. Illustrations of the IPA. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(2): 511–531. doi:10.1017/S0025100321000177
new_statements.locator: 'Prosody' section, FirstView pp. 17–18 (pdf pp. 18–19 of the saved repository copy; ≈ pp. 527–528 in the printed 53(2) pagination, offset not verified)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The two first-hand descriptions disagree. The reference grammar (Thieberger 2006: 65–66, saved) says stress is non-contrastive and that initial stress is the dominant pattern for monomorphemic roots, with lexical exceptions (na-initial nouns stressed on the syllable after na-; some plant names penultimate). The instrumental work by the same team (JASA 2020; JIPA Illustration 2023) finds instead a consistent right-edge (word-final) f0 prominence, independent of vowel length/syllable weight, with vowel deletion targeting the pre-tonic penult, and suggests this prominence is a phrasal (accentual-phrase) boundary tone rather than lexical stress. The most recent authoritative description therefore treats the lexical-stress analysis as superseded but leaves the word-level pattern open ('research... ongoing').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Thieberger 2006: 65–66: words with article na- stress the first syllable following na- (na.'fa.nu 'heaven'); some na- words take initial stress ('na.ta.mol 'person'); multisyllabic plant names show penultimate stress (nau.'?a.las); suffixation re-assigns stress and destresses/deletes medial vowels (p. 69). JIPA 2023 / IJL 2020: prominence location may shift under pragmatic/focus conditions, e.g. in non-focal contexts (Fletcher et al. 2019). Early 2007 review: reviewer heard final stress where the grammar records initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Grammar statement is impressionistic, about citation-form monomorphemic words from recordings. Instrumental results are for di-/trisyllabic words in an utterance-medial carrier frame; the right-edge prominence is argued to be phrasal (accentual phrase boundary tone) rather than word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Nafsan = South Efate (sout2856, ISO erk) as spoken in Erakor (primary), Eratap and Pango villages; Thieberger's corpus and the phonetic studies are Erakor-based. Not to be confused with the 'compromise literary dialect' of Macdonald 1907 or with Efate/North Efate (Nakanamanga, efat1235 / nort2836).

sources.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas. 2006. A Grammar of South Efate: An Oceanic Language of Vanuatu. Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 33. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. xxviii+384 pp.
sources.note: §3.5.4 Stress, pp. 65–66 (pdf pp. 93–94): 'Stress is not contrastive in South Efate.' Initial stress is the dominant pattern for monomorphemic roots (ex. 35–36a); words with the article na- stress the first syllable after na- (36b), some na- words have initial stress (36c), and a group of multisyllabic plant names has penultimate stress (36d). Suffixation re-assigns stress and destresses/deletes medial vowels (§3.6.1, p. 69).

sources.note: §3.5.4 Stress (pdf p. 102): same text as the 2006 grammar — 'Stress is not contrastive in South Efate'; examples of monomorphemic stems 'all show initial stress'. Superseded by the 2006 published version.

sources.citation: Billington, Rosey, Janet Fletcher, Nick Thieberger & Ben Volchok. 2020. Acoustic evidence for right-edge prominence in Nafsan. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 147(4): 2829–2844. doi:10.1121/10.0000995
sources.note: Instrumental study of disyllabic and trisyllabic words in a carrier frame. Lit. summary (p. 2831): previous sources lack 'consensus on where, or whether, there is consistent stress placement within a word. Suggested patterns include both final stress and initial stress, with some lexically-specified differences (Capell, 1935-1980; Thieberger, 2006)'. Conclusions (p. 2838): 'compelling evidence that Nafsan words tend to be produced with greater prominence at the right edge'; final-syllable f0 13–21 Hz higher than preceding syllables; results 'accord with impressions of final prominence in Nafs…

sources.citation: Billington, Rosey, Nick Thieberger & Janet Fletcher. 2020. Phonetic evidence for phonotactic change in Nafsan (South Efate). Italian Journal of Linguistics 32(1): 123–148.
sources.note: §4 Prominence patterns (pp. 132–133): previous work gives 'impressions of non-contrastive stress... without a consensus on which syllable within a word is most prominent'; experimental results 'show a strong preference for prominence at the right edge of the word', short and long final vowels alike, 'suggesting that syllable weight is not a factor'; main correlate f0; the right-edge prominence 'may relate to phrasal rather than lexical constituents' (post-lexical high boundary tones). §5.1: medial vowel deletion is pre-tonic. Notes that Clark 1985: 20, Lynch 2000a: 333 and Thieberger 2006: 67…

sources.citation: Fletcher, Janet, Rosey Billington & Nick Thieberger. 2019. Prosodic marking of focus in Nafsan. Proceedings of the 19th ICPhS, Melbourne, 3787–3791.
sources.note: Intro: 'Nafsan has previously been analysed as a stress language although this is still under investigation'; the paper is about focus intonation (rising f0 at word right edge as accentual-phrase boundary), not word stress.

sources.citation: Early, Robert. 2007. Review of A Grammar of South Efate: An Oceanic Language of Vanuatu. Language Documentation & Conservation 1(1).
sources.note: Reviewer remarks that 'Noninstrumental perceptions of stress can vary: where T. heard ˈmet.ma.tur (65), I heard met.ma.ˈtur, and where he heard ˈnrae.na.tu (66), I heard nrae.na.ˈtu' — i.e. the reviewer perceived final stress where the grammar records initial stress.
